parsed.title: Off the Rails: Inside an Exposed Silent Lynx Server
parsed.summary: Silent Lynx, a Central Asia-focused espionage cluster, was exposed through an open directory on a server that CloudSEK analysed, covering activity from April to October 2026. The directory held implant builds for Laplas and Chvost families, delivery kits built on LNK shortcuts and PowerShell reverse shells, and victim data. The operator had domain-level access to Tajikistan's national railway and used one compromised railway employee account to pull thousands of government documents, many tied to the Ministry of Defence, from Tajikistan's document management platform. Intrusions also reached an Uzbek GeoServer host, and lures impersonating Turkmen railway and regional administration bodies pointed to a planned campaign against Turkmenistan. The operator ran much of the work through a self-hosted DeepSeek-based AI agent, and test sessions from a residential Kazakh ISP connection support a medium-confidence Kazakhstan nexus.

parsed.title: Trigram Campaign
parsed.summary: Stormshield attributes the Trigram campaign with high confidence to North Korea, as a continuation of the UNK_DeadDrop cluster and the Kimsuky group. The actors impersonate about 50 brands in the blockchain, AI, and logistics sectors through fake recruitment, conference invitation, and package-tracking sites. Victims are tricked via a ClickFix-style fake verification step into pasting a command that is silently swapped in the clipboard to download and run a malicious script. The payload is a JavaScript loader that deploys an infostealer targeting browser credentials and cryptocurrency wallets. A campaign management platform automates GitHub-based target collection, bulk email delivery across four providers, and real-time victim tracking.

parsed.title: Analysis of a Wpcdoor Attack Distributed Through Domestic DVR Management Software
parsed.summary: The Wpcdoor backdoor was distributed through the CMS (Central Management Software) of a domestic Korean DVR and CCTV vendor, as reported by Huntress and confirmed by AhnLab's ASD logs showing infections in Korea. The attack chain runs through rs.win32.exe, where a malicious IPHLPAPI.DLL is side-loaded and acts as a downloader for WpcMon.exe and samcli.dll, which in turn fetches the final Wpcdoor backdoor and runs it in memory. Wpcdoor can steal system information, capture screenshots and clipboard data, grab files, dump browser data and cryptocurrency wallet-related memory, and enable remote control. AhnLab tracks the actor as Larva-26013, which has also deployed Wpcdoor in other campaigns. Defenders should apply vendor patches, review the configuration of the affected software, and immediately change IDs and passwords used in the software and connected systems.

parsed.title: The XG Files: Falcon C2 Flying Under The (Browser) Radar
parsed.summary: Unit 42 describes Falcon (aka XG), a NodeJS command and control framework that compromises browsers by running malicious JavaScript on webmail and government web applications. The framework can sideload a malicious Chrome extension disguised as a PDF viewer to steal passwords, emails, session cookies and communications. Falcon also delivers the Rust-based Antino implant, which uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 channel. Campaigns between March and May 2026 compromised government entities in one Middle Eastern country and several Southeast Asian countries, targeting foreign affairs, defense, interior and law enforcement ministries. Defenders should monitor for developer-mode extensions with broad permissions, unexpected Hm_lvt_ cookies, and unfamiliar external script tags on internal portals.

parsed.title: Beyond the Signature: How Attackers Hide Malware in PE Certificate Tables
parsed.summary: Morphisec researchers describe a finance-themed campaign, distributed via WhatsApp and email archives with invoice and account-adjustment lures, that delivers a modular encrypted backdoor. Two alternative loaders converge on Donut-based execution: one side-loads a malicious dbghelp.dll beside a Tencent-signed executable and downloads shellcode for Early Bird APC injection into mspaint.exe. The newer variant hides an RC4-encrypted payload in the PE certificate-table region of a modified Kingsoft/WPS DLL and runs it via in-process APC. The implant communicates over AES-256-GCM-protected TCP, profiles hosts, monitors user activity, and loads C2-delivered PE modules for persistence and remote desktop. Defenders should correlate suspicious side-loaded DLLs, unexpected PE security-directory data, and APC-based execution rather than trusting signed hosts alone.

parsed.title: Field Intelligence #5: Scareware at scale. Investment scams built on AI platforms.
parsed.summary: ZoidWays is a mobile scareware forced-redirect campaign tracked since March, reaching about 1.5 million blocked impressions in one day across at least six ad buying platforms. Victims see a fake phone-settings clone with a bogus "Platform Security for wiretapping" alert that leads to antivirus checkouts, paid support lines, or subscription traps. The report also covers a fake Microsoft Teams APK that functions as a remote access trojan, harvesting cryptocurrency seed phrases via clipboard, filesystem, and OCR scanning. PseudoCamo runs investment scams on AI app-builder platforms, with cloaked age-gate landing pages that redirect to second-hop money pages across multiple countries. D-Shortiez has shifted its tech-support scams to BunnyCDN and Azure hosts and added a fake CAPTCHA step that resembles ClickFix but is a forced redirect. A Claude-branded "trading bot" scam tricks UK victims into moving their own funds through a MetaMask contract that forwards the balance to the scammer.

parsed.title: Inside The Server: 14 Months of Offensive Cyber Operations Targeting Europe
parsed.summary: Group-IB discovered an open directory on a Latvian server exposing the working environment of a threat actor it tracks as DarkLunnen, containing over 14 months of offensive operations against Europe. The operator, apparently still active at discovery, used a modified watchTowr proof-of-concept for FortiGate CVE-2024-55591 to create a backdoor "service" super-admin account across devices in Turkey, Ukraine, Azerbaijan, and Algeria. Other activity included VNC brute-forcing that reached apparent HMI systems, scanning of Hikvision cameras, and attempted source code collection from Ukrainian defense and aviation organizations. Group-IB has not attributed the operator to a known actor, and only 35 of 457 files were recovered. Defenders should patch edge devices, rotate secrets on any exposed device, and restrict VNC, camera, and remote management interfaces.

parsed.title: Online Casino Serves Malicious Python SDK
parsed.summary: The malicious PyPI package aurum-pay (version 1.2.0) presents itself as a working payment SDK for an online casino, but its first real API request silently fetches a command from the casino's domain and runs it. On Linux, that command downloads and launches "RCMD Remote Agent," a remote access trojan that installs persistence as a fake Chromium systemd service. The trojan connects to a hard-coded controller and gives the operator shell access, file transfer, reconnaissance, and screenshots. Because the SDK's default host also receives API keys and customer payment data, applications using the package may have exposed sensitive information as well. Defenders should assume compromise of any host that ran aurum-pay and check for the listed persistence files and network connections.

parsed.title: The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2
parsed.summary: Threat actors are deploying GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers to keep access after the original web application vulnerabilities are patched. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. Microsoft Defender telemetry shows detections rising 356.2% from March through August 2026, concentrated on PHP web applications and cPanel hosting. Education and research accounted for the largest share of affected organizations at 30.7%. Defenders should remediate the host by removing the GSocket client, persistence, and staged files, and constrain outbound traffic rather than relying on application patching alone.

parsed.title: Citrus Ransomware: VLESS for traffic, Sn00py for encryption, and LLMs lending a hand
parsed.summary: Citrus Ransomware is a previously undocumented Russian-speaking group that targets Russian companies only, and it gains access through compromised contractor accounts used over corporate VPNs or internet-facing RDP. The group uses LLM-generated commands and scripts, identifiable by typical LLM comments, and tunnels traffic through Xray VLESS with REALITY to mimic HTTPS. It escalates privileges by exploiting the Certighost authentication bypass (CVE-2026-54121) and disables Windows Defender and other security tools via malicious Group Policy Objects. Its Sn00py-family ransomware, distributed as ransomware-as-a-service, encrypts user files with RSA-2048 and ChaCha20 and skips domain controllers so the policy keeps spreading. Defenders should tightly control contractor access, since compromised contractor accounts are how attackers get in.

parsed.title: Beware of phishing emails disguised as quote requests (SnakeKeylogger)
parsed.summary: Phishing emails impersonating a purchasing department materials staffer and disguised as quote requests are distributing SnakeKeylogger, an infostealer. The email lures the recipient into downloading a compressed archive containing a JavaScript file, which decrypts and runs an obfuscated PowerShell script. That script uses AES-256-CBC and XOR decryption to load the final payload in memory and injects it into aspnet_compiler.exe via process hollowing. SnakeKeylogger collects browser-stored data, system information, and keystrokes, then exfiltrates them over SMTP or Telegram. Defenders should verify sender domains, check for suspicious file extensions such as .js or .exe, and confirm URLs before entering sensitive information.

parsed.title: Malware Must Die!: MMD-0070-2026 - Once upon a time, Linux/Hajime hexstring-pushed a tiny ARM ELF fileless downloader
parsed.summary: Linux/Hajime is an IoT botnet that spreads through three propagation methods, including a 480-byte ARM ELF downloader delivered via hexstring pushing that uses socketcall to evade ptrace-based tracing. The downloader fetches a custom-packed 80280-byte payload, then deletes itself after dropping it. Once unpacked, the main bot disables the hardware watchdog, renames itself to look like telnetd, adds iptables DROP rules for ports 23, 7547, 5555 and 5358, and force-kills processes listed in /proc/net/tcp. It maintains BitTorrent DHT and NTP routines for lookups, which gives it a peer-to-peer design with no fixed C2 to block. The author notes 3,029 infected IPs across 111 countries, with Taiwan and South Korea leading. Defenders should close exposed Telnet, TR-069 and similar services, patch device firmware, and watch for unexpected DHT traffic and firewall rules from IoT segments.

parsed.title: Analysis of APT-C-35 (Donot) group attack activity against Pakistan using holiday-themed lures
parsed.summary: APT-C-35 (Donot), a South Asia-focused espionage group, was observed by 360 Advanced Threat Research Institute using a malicious Excel macro document disguised as an Eid-ul-Adha invitation. The macro loads multi-stage shellcode that decrypts data via NOT and XOR operations, checks for security product drivers, and downloads a DLL disguised with an MP3 extension after repairing its PE header. The DLL persists through a scheduled task that runs rundll32, then uploads host information such as username, computer name, and installed software to a C2 server using AES-128-CBC encryption and Base64 encoding. The C2 server selectively delivers follow-on plugins, so the operators may tailor payloads to specific victims, which limited the researchers' full view. Targets were Pakistan-based, and the group's reuse of prior TTPs, such as macro structure, URL patterns, and DLL header fixes, supported attribution. Defenders should treat unsolicited attachments and links with caution, especially document lures tied to current events.

parsed.title: Trading User Risk Alert: Counterfeit MetaTrader Installer Bundles Rust Malware to Deliver the Silver Fox Backdoor
parsed.summary: Rising's threat intelligence team reports a campaign targeting traders with counterfeit MetaTrader installers that bundle a Rust downloader with a legitimately signed MetaTrader 4 setup. The downloader runs in the background while the genuine installer is displayed to distract the user. It establishes persistence through a logon scheduled task or logon script, depending on privileges, and retrieves a loader that fetches a Silver Fox remote access module. That module supports command execution, file management, screen capture, keylogging, and clipboard access. The report links the activity to the Silver Fox ecosystem based on several distinctive traits. Defenders should block social-engineered installer bundles and monitor for in-memory loading and unexpected logon persistence.

parsed.title: ZeroQlik Returns: Exploiting N-Days Still Pays Off
parsed.summary: Cynet researchers observed a PowerShell reverse shell on Qlik Sense servers at several EU-based customers in October 2026, launched under scheduler.exe in a pattern resembling the 2023 Cactus ransomware intrusions. The activity likely exploited Qlik Sense vulnerabilities CVE-2023-41266, CVE-2023-41265, or CVE-2023-48365, though the exact vulnerability remains unconfirmed. An open directory on the same server hosted Go-based backdoors for Windows and Linux, persistence scripts, and ActiveMQ and Veeam exploit material, which appeared to be in testing. The attacker ran discovery commands and persistence tasks, including SSH key installation and a scheduled task. Cynet blocked the initial script, and no successful ActiveMQ exploitation was observed.

parsed.title: CookUp follow-up: nine signing companies and 25 C2 domains behind the “useful app” installers
parsed.summary: The CookUp campaign is a cluster of signed "useful app" installers that a server-side decision gates, and the same loader has now been tied to installers signed by nine companies. The installers contact 25 command-and-control domains, all behind Cloudflare, with lures that include recipe apps, PDF tools, game cheats, and generic "download ready" pages. Several antivirus vendors label these installers as TamperedChef. The app-themed ones install a working app, and the final payload has not been observed because the servers refused to deliver it. Defenders are advised to block the domains, hunt for files from the listed signers, and treat any Document_, PDF_, or CookingApp_-named executable as a program rather than a document.
